title: What Programmers Get Wrong About AI
author: Managing The Future
summary: Managing The Future challenges the common inference that if AI can replace elite programmers, no knowledge job is safe, arguing this treats every profession as measurable on a single axis of raw intelligence rather than recognizing what actually made programming an easy early target: text-based work, enormous training data, and unusually fast, objective feedback (code compiles or it doesn't). The piece contrasts this with accountants and CEOs, whose hardest decisions, whether a reserve is prudent, which strategy to commit capital to, have no test suite and no clean answer key, meaning AI automates the parts of those jobs with fast feedback while leaving judgment-under-uncertainty squarely with humans. For CEOs specifically, the useful question isn't which jobs AI eliminates but where an organization's feedback loops are fast and objective versus slow and contested, since that predicts where AI will actually take over work. The piece closes by insisting AI can be an excellent thinking partner for a leader but remains structurally incapable of owning accountability for a decision.
points: The core reframe is a category error diagnosis: assuming all jobs sit on a single 'intelligence required' axis, so if AI beats elite programmers it must beat everyone, ignores that programming's real vulnerability was fast, objective feedback (compiles or breaks), not raw difficulty.

The diagnostic question the piece offers leaders is concrete and transferable: 'How quickly and objectively can we tell whether the work was done well?' — fast/clear feedback predicts rapid AI automation, slow/contested feedback predicts persistent human judgment responsibility.

The accountant example sharpens the point precisely: arithmetic was automated long ago, but deciding whether a contract's revenue recognition timing is aggressive or prudent has 'no test suite for materiality,' which is exactly the kind of judgment AI cannot grade itself on.

The piece draws a hard line for leaders: AI can serve as a thinking partner that surfaces assumptions and second-order consequences, but it 'cannot carry the accountability' of a strategic decision — the CEO must still make the call and earn the organization's commitment to it.
quotes: The problem is that many of the people making sweeping forecasts about the future of work have spent their careers doing one particular kind of work, the exact kind of work that AI got good at first.

AI has been strongest in the parts of programming with clear inputs, clear outputs, and fast feedback. It has been less reliable at deciding what the company should build, why it should build it, and what tradeoffs it should make.
That kind of work does not grade itself. There is no test suite for materiality. There is no clean answer key for professional judgment under uncertainty.
The question that best indicates which jobs will be affected most is: How quickly and objectively can we tell whether the work was done well?

But AI is an input, not an owner. It cannot carry the accountability of choosing a strategy, hiring an executive, committing capital, or deciding which stakeholder interest should prevail when they conflict.
We should take technologists' warnings seriously while recognizing that their experience with code is not a complete theory of the future of work.
